column1: What's the difference between a detection control and a prevention control for cost governance?
column2: Detection tells you something happened after the fact (a notification); prevention stops it from happening (e.g. auto-destroy). This project deliberately chose detection-only, since auto-remediation's failure mode (destroying real work-in-progress on a false positive) is worse than the cost risk it solves for a single-learner lab.

column1: Why does aws_cloudwatch_event_target exist as a separate resource from aws_cloudwatch_event_rule?
column2: A single EventBridge rule can fan out to multiple targets. Splitting rule and target into separate resources lets one schedule notify several different destinations without duplicating the rule.

column1: Which argument enables or disables an aws_cloudwatch_event_rule, and which older argument does it replace?
column2: state (a string, ENABLED or DISABLED) is the current argument. It replaces is_enabled, a boolean that is deprecated — don't copy is_enabled forward from older examples.

column1: What are the two accepted forms of schedule_expression on an EventBridge rule?
column2: A rate expression, e.g. rate(1 hour), or a cron expression, e.g. cron(0 12 * * ? *). A rule uses either schedule_expression or event_pattern — this demo uses the schedule form.

column1: Is notification on aws_budgets_budget a list argument or a repeatable block?
column2: A repeatable block — write one notification block per independent threshold (e.g. 50% and 80%), each with its own comparison_operator, threshold, and subscriber list.

column1: What's the difference between notification_type = ACTUAL and FORECASTED on an AWS Budget?
column2: ACTUAL alerts based on money already spent. FORECASTED alerts based on a projected spending trend, before the actual threshold is crossed — a more proactive but less literal signal.

column1: What type is limit_amount on aws_budgets_budget?
column2: A string, not a number — e.g. limit_amount = \50\". A variable feeding it should be declared type = string to match the provider schema."

column1: When would you use a standalone aws_sns_topic_policy instead of the inline policy argument on aws_sns_topic?
column2: When the policy needs to reference a resource that doesn't exist yet at the point the topic is declared — such as an EventBridge rule's ARN used in an aws:SourceArn condition. Both produce a resource-based policy on the topic.

column1: An SNS topic policy grants Principal = { Service = \events.amazonaws.com\" } with no Condition block. What's the practical effect?"
column2: Any EventBridge rule in the account could publish to that topic, not just the intended one. Adding an ArnEquals condition on aws:SourceArn narrows it to one specific rule. Omitting it isn't an error — it silently widens the policy.

column1: How do you encrypt an aws_sns_topic at rest using a free, AWS managed key?
column2: Set kms_master_key_id = \alias/aws/sns\". Storage of an AWS managed key is always free; only API requests against it are billed

column1: What is the cost difference between an AWS managed KMS key and a customer managed KMS key?
column2: AWS managed key storage is free (API calls beyond the free tier are billed separately). A customer managed key costs a flat $1/month regardless of use, plus API call charges.

column1: Why did this demo fix checkov's CKV_AWS_26 finding (unencrypted SNS topic) instead of adding it to skip-check?
column2: Because the fix (an AWS managed KMS key) is free and a one-line change — skip-check is for findings that are genuinely out of scope or involve a real trade-off, not a default response to any finding.

column1: What happens if tflint's .tflint.hcl sets source on a plugin block without also setting version?
column2: tflint --init fails outright with an error that version cannot be omitted when source is specified — this is not an optional convenience, it's a hard requirement.

column1: Why does an SNS email subscription created by Terraform still show PendingConfirmation, and why doesn't terraform plan flag it?
column2: Email subscriptions require the recipient to click a confirmation link. That confirmation state lives in AWS, not in the Terraform configuration, so plan reports no changes while the subscription sits unusable.

column1: Are tflint and checkov Terraform provisioners?
column2: No. Both are external CLI tools that read .tf files directly off disk and report findings, entirely outside the plan/apply cycle. They should run before a real apply, not be wired into a resource's lifecycle.

column1: Does terraform validate catch every provider-specific value constraint, like an incorrectly-cased enum string?
column2: No. validate checks structure and schema (correct block shape, required arguments present) but not every value-level constraint the provider enforces — some invalid values pass validate and plan, and only fail at apply against the real AWS API.

column1: How many new resources should an incremental terraform apply report when only one new resource block was added to an already-applied config?
column2: Exactly one — the count reflects what that specific apply changes, not the configuration's running total. Outputs aren't counted. A larger reported count against already-existing state is a signal to inspect the plan before confirming.

column1: What happens if a terraform.tfvars value is set for a variable that hasn't been declared yet?
column2: Terraform issues a 'Value for undeclared variable' warning at init, validate, and plan — the apply itself isn't blocked, but it's a workflow smell worth fixing by declaring the variable before setting its value.

column1: Does demo 22b create its own state backend?
column2: No — it reuses 22a's own backend.tf unchanged, pointing at the platform/terraform.tfstate key in the bucket 22a bootstrapped. 22b is simply the first config to write real resources into that key.

column1: Why is 22b's Cleanup a verification step rather than terraform destroy?
column2: Its resources are free or near-free governance controls meant to protect every subsequent session, and its state is shared within the platform tier with 22c and Demo 24 once those exist — a destroy here would take down all of them at once for no cost benefit.
